items.title: The Arctic warms roughly 4 times faster than the global average

options.text: The Arctic warms at the same rate as the tropics
The Arctic has warmed roughly 4 times the global mean since 1979 (Rantanen et al., 2022), driven by ice-albedo feedback, water-vapour feedback and changes in heat transport

items.reveal:
Mika Rantanen and colleagues (Communications Earth & Environment, 2022) revised the long-cited 2× figure to nearly 4× for the Arctic Circle since 1979.

Ice-albedo feedback: snow and ice reflect around 80% of incoming solar radiation; open ocean absorbs around 90%. As sea ice retreats, more energy is absorbed and warming accelerates.

Arctic sea ice extent in September has fallen from around 7 million km² (1979 average) to under 4 million km² (recent minima). Downstream effects include changes to jet stream behaviour, ocean stratification and methane release from thawing permafrost.
items.why: Average warming hides extreme regional warming. The Arctic case shows how feedbacks multiply local signals — and why polar regions are decisive for global climate trajectory.

items.title: A 4-figure grid reference is precise to 1 km; a 6-figure to 100 m
items.claim: What precision does each give on a UK Ordnance Survey map?

options.text: 4-figure references identify a 1 km × 1 km square; 6-figure references identify a 100 m × 100 m square. 8-figure references give 10 m precision
References are accurate to 1 metre regardless

items.reveal:
OS uses a National Grid: read eastings (left-right) first, then northings (bottom-up). 'Along the corridor, then up the stairs.'

Grid letters (SE, NY etc.) identify 100 km squares. A full reference combines letters with numerical eastings/northings — e.g. SE 5436 (4-figure within the SE square, locating a 1 km grid square; SE 543 367 for 6-figure 100 m precision).

The National Grid covers Great Britain only; Northern Ireland uses the Irish Grid. GPS coordinates (latitude/longitude or UTM) are international alternatives.
items.why: Map references are not arbitrary precision. Reporting weather or accident locations using inconsistent precision causes real navigation failures — including search-and-rescue.
